learn.hook: Your aunt says 'Take Science, beta, it has more jobs'. Your friend's parents say 'Arts is fine for a girl'. Sounds like personal advice? Sociology says it is society talking through them.
points: Everyday advice to students (study hard, pick a job-oriented subject, choose what is 'suitable' for a girl or a boy, follow family expectations) shows that individual choices are shaped by social forces.
Results depend on effort, but also on things outside one person's control: the job market, gender, family background and social class.
Sociology asks questions about meanings we take for granted, such as who decides what a 'good job' or a 'good subject' is, and why.

Key terms: social constraint (society limits and pressures our choices), values (shared ideas of what is good or desirable) and empirical investigation (finding out by observing evidence, not by guessing).
The chapter previews: the sociological imagination, plurality and inequality, what sociology is, how it grew in Europe and India, and its scope and links with other social sciences.

example.q: Meera scored well but chose Commerce because 'an uncle said CA pays well', while her brother was told engineering was 'made for boys'. Use sociology to explain their choices.
steps: Notice the advice is not purely personal: it comes from family and relatives.
Link it to the job market: some careers are seen as 'paying well'.
Link it to gender: some fields are labelled as suitable for boys or girls.
Conclude that social forces (market, gender, family expectations) shaped choices that looked individual.
example.answer: Their 'personal' choices were shaped by social forces such as the job market, gender expectations and family values.

learn.reallife: Every year lakhs of students crowd coaching hubs like Kota for engineering and medical entrance exams. Sociologists study why certain careers become 'prestigious' and how family background and class affect who can afford such coaching.

games.title: Match the key term
pairs: Pressure from society that limits our choices
Shared ideas of what is good or desirable
Finding out by observing actual evidence
Position based on wealth, income and occupation

games.title: Choices: personal or social?
items: A student's choice of subject can be influenced by the job market.
Demand for certain jobs shapes which subjects seem 'useful'.
Sociology says success depends only on individual hard work.
Effort matters, but gender, class and family background also shape outcomes.
Labelling some subjects as 'suitable for girls' is an example of a social force acting on choices.
Gender expectations are social, not natural.
Sociology accepts ideas like 'a good job' without questioning them.
Sociology asks who defines a 'good job' and why.
Family background can affect a student's educational opportunities.
Resources and expectations differ across families and classes.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the sociological view of a student's career choice?
options: It depends only on the student's own intelligence and marks
It is shaped by both individual effort and wider social forces
It is decided purely by luck, so there is nothing to explain
It is fixed at birth by nature and cannot change at all
quiz.explain: Sociology recognises individual effort but shows how the job market, gender, class and family also shape choices.
quiz.mistake: Treats individual choice as completely separate from society

quiz.q: 'Arts is a good subject for girls; boys should do engineering.' Sociologically, this advice reflects:
options: A biological fact about ability
The student's personal hobby
A government rule
Gender expectations in society
quiz.explain: Linking subjects to gender is a social expectation, not a natural law.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes a social stereotype for a natural fact

quiz.q: A sociologist asks, 'Who decides what counts as a good job?' This shows that sociology:
options: Questions meanings that people take for granted
Gives practical career advice to students and parents
Only collects statistics about jobs and salaries
Accepts popular opinion as the truth about jobs
quiz.explain: Sociology examines everyday assumptions and asks where they come from.

quiz.q: Finding out by observing and checking actual evidence is called:
options: Philosophical reflection
Common sense
Empirical investigation
Moral judgement
quiz.explain: Empirical means based on observation and evidence that others can check.
quiz.mistake: Confuses empirical work with armchair thinking

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the social factors that can affect a student's success?
options: The social class of the student's family
Gender expectations at home and school
The colour of the student's school bag
Demand for certain skills in the job market
quiz.explain: Class, gender and job markets are social forces; a bag's colour is irrelevant.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks that class, gender and market are all social forces

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The advice students receive about subjects is often shaped by the job market.
Reason (R): Subjects linked to well-paid jobs are usually seen as more 'useful' by families.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the perceived link between subjects and good jobs explains why the market shapes advice.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see R as the reason behind A

quiz.q: Case: Ravi, from a family that cannot afford coaching, fails to clear an entrance exam that his richer classmate clears. A sociologist would most likely point to:
options: Ravi's own laziness, with no other factor involved
Bad luck on the exam day and nothing else
The exam being too easy for the richer student
Unequal access to resources linked to social class
quiz.explain: Sociology looks at structured differences such as class, which affect who can pay for coaching.

quiz.q: 'Social constraint' refers to:
options: A written law passed by Parliament or a state assembly
The ways society limits and pressures individual choices
A person's physical weakness or illness that limits work
A shortage of goods in the market that limits buying
quiz.explain: Social constraint is pressure from social norms, institutions and expectations on what we do.
quiz.mistake: Thinks constraint means only formal law

teach.ask: Gappu wants to become a pilot but his uncle says 'Pilots are boys, study home science'. Explain to Gappu how society shapes such 'personal' choices.
teach.praise: Tweet! So my choice is mine, but society keeps whispering in my ear. Now I can question that whisper!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but what outside my own effort is shaping this advice? Think gender, class and jobs.

topics.title: The sociological imagination: troubles and issues

learn.hook: One person losing a job is bad luck. Thirty out of every hundred losing jobs at once is something else entirely. C. Wright Mills gave us the lens to see the difference.
points: C. Wright Mills, an American sociologist, called it the sociological imagination: the ability to grasp the link between a person's biography and the wider history of society.
Personal troubles of the milieu: problems within a person's own life and immediate relations (one person unemployed).
Public issues of social structure: problems that go beyond individuals and arise from how society is organised (mass unemployment, war, industrialisation).

Homelessness looks like private hardship, but it is often a public issue linked to lack of jobs, low wages and rural-urban migration. The state responds with schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (rural housing).
Exercise skill: take a personal problem (yours or someone's) and trace the public issue behind it.

example.q: Mills wrote that if one man in a city of 1,00,000 is unemployed, it is a personal trouble; but if 15 million out of 50 million employees are unemployed, it is an issue. What percentage is unemployed in the second case, and why is it a public issue?
steps: Unemployment rate = 15 ÷ 50 × 100
When almost a third of workers are jobless, the cause cannot lie in each person's character.
The cause lies in the structure of the economy, so it is a public issue.
example.answer: 30%; it is a public issue because the cause lies in the economic structure, not in individuals.

learn.reallife: During the 2020 lockdown, lakhs of migrant workers walked home from cities like Delhi and Mumbai. Each family's struggle was a personal trouble, but together they revealed a public issue: insecure informal work and weak social security.

options: C. Wright Mills
Auguste Comte
Max Weber
M.N. Srinivas
quiz.explain: Mills used the term for linking personal biography to wider history and social structure.
quiz.mistake: Credits any famous sociologist without recalling the concept's author

quiz.q: The sociological imagination helps us to grasp the relationship between:
options: Body and mind
Religion and science
Biography and history
Village and forest
quiz.explain: Mills said it lets us see how individual lives connect with large-scale social change.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a psychological or philosophical pairing

quiz.q: In Mills' terms, mass unemployment caused by an economic slump is a:
options: Personal trouble of the milieu
Public issue of social structure
Natural disaster
Private moral failure
quiz.explain: When many are affected and the cause lies in the economy, it is a public issue.
quiz.mistake: Treats a widespread structural problem as an individual one

quiz.q: A country has 50 million employees, and 15 million are unemployed. What percentage are unemployed?
quiz.explain: 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. Mills used this kind of figure to show unemployment as a public issue.
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way round or forgets to multiply by 100

quiz.q: Why does sociology treat homelessness as more than a personal hardship?
options: Homeless people have mostly chosen to live that way
It affects only one person at a time, never many
It is caused by bad weather and natural events alone
It is linked to lack of jobs and rural-urban migration
quiz.explain: Many homeless people move to cities seeking work; housing shortages and low wages are structural causes.
quiz.mistake: Explains homelessness only through individual choice

quiz.q: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin is an example of:
options: A personal trouble of one family's milieu
A state response to a public issue of housing
A private charity run by a religious trust
A loan scheme run by private banks for profit
quiz.explain: The state treats housing shortage as a public issue and runs schemes to address it.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect public issues with state policy

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): War is a public issue in Mills' sense.
Reason (R): War changes the lives of vast numbers of people through forces far beyond any one person's control.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; war is a public issue precisely because its causes and effects lie in large-scale structures.
quiz.mistake: Thinks R is unrelated to why war counts as a public issue

quiz.q: Case: Sunita's father lost his job when the mill in their town shut down along with three others. Using the sociological imagination, Sunita should see this as:
options: Part of a wider change in industry affecting many families
A sign that her father personally did not work hard enough
Purely a family matter with no social causes behind it
An event that is too personal for anyone to study
quiz.explain: Several mills closing points to a structural change; her family's trouble is linked to a public issue.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the wider pattern behind a personal event

teach.ask: Gappu's cousin lost his job and feels ashamed. Explain to Gappu, using Mills' idea, how a personal trouble can be a public issue.
teach.praise: Chirp! So one person's problem can be a window onto a society-wide issue. The sociological imagination is like binoculars!
teach.nudge: But how many people are affected, and is the cause inside the person or in society? Use Mills' two terms.

learn.hook: Ask 'Which society do you belong to?' and you may answer Indian, Tamil, a cricket fan, a city kid and a member of your community all at once. Each answer is right, depending on the situation.
points: We each belong to many 'societies' at once: nation, language, region, religion, caste, tribe and more. Which one we call 'ours' depends on context.
India shows plurality: village and city, older and newer traditions, and many groups living side by side.
Societies are also unequal: groups have unequal access to wealth, education, health, power and respect. Inequality exists both between and within societies.

Discrimination can occur in daily life, for example a Dalit person being refused equal service at a village tea shop. Such practices are illegal and violate the Constitution, yet sociology studies why they persist.

Amartya Sen stressed that inequality has many dimensions beyond income, such as health, education and freedom. Survey data like the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) give indicators, e.g. access to sanitation.

example.q: NFHS-style data show that 90% of households in District A but only 45% in District B have improved toilets. What does a sociologist conclude?
steps: Identify the indicator: access to sanitation.
Compare: District A has double the access of District B (90 ÷ 45 = 2).
Recognise this as unequal access to a basic service.
Look for social causes: income, region, caste or gender differences, and public provision.
example.answer: Sanitation access is unequal; the gap is an indicator of inequality that needs social explanation.

learn.reallife: Large surveys such as the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and Census of India data help policy-makers see where clean water, toilets or schooling are lacking, so schemes like Swachh Bharat can target them.

items: A person can belong to several 'societies' at the same time.

quiz.q: Which statement about belonging to 'a society' is correct?
options: Each person belongs to only one society for the whole of life
A person belongs to several societies, and context decides which matters
Society means only the nation-state of which one is a citizen
Belonging to a society is decided only by the place where one was born
quiz.explain: People belong to nation, language, region, religion and other groupings at once.
quiz.mistake: Assumes 'society' is a single fixed unit

quiz.q: India's plurality refers to:
options: Rule by many political parties at the same time in different states
The very large size of India's population alone
Having many states and union territories only
The coexistence of many groups, traditions and ways of life
quiz.explain: Plurality means diversity of groups, languages, traditions, and village and city life.
quiz.mistake: Reduces plurality to a single political or numerical fact

quiz.q: Sociologically, inequality means:
options: Unequal access of groups to resources such as wealth, education, health and power
Natural differences in height, strength and talent between individual people
People choosing different hobbies, tastes and lifestyles freely
Groups following different customs, foods and festivals
quiz.explain: Inequality is structured unequal access to valued resources and respect.

quiz.q: The idea that inequality has many dimensions beyond income is associated with:
options: Herbert Spencer
Auguste Comte
Amartya Sen
Ferdinand Tönnies
quiz.explain: Sen argued that well-being includes health, education and freedoms, not only income.
quiz.mistake: Picks a classical thinker unconnected with this idea

quiz.q: District A has 90% households with toilets and District B has 45%. Access in A is how many times that in B?
quiz.explain: 90 ÷ 45 = 2, so A has double the access: a clear inequality indicator.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing, or divides the wrong way

quiz.q: Case: In a village, a Dalit man is served tea in a separate cup at a tea stall. Sociologically, this shows:
options: Caste-based discrimination in everyday life
A personal taste in crockery of the stall owner
An equal and fair practice followed for all customers
A rule of good hygiene that applies to everyone
quiz.explain: Separate treatment on the basis of caste denies equal respect; it is discrimination and is unlawful.
quiz.mistake: Explains discrimination away as a neutral custom

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Inequality exists within societies as well as between them.
Reason (R): All members of a society have exactly equal access to resources.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: A is true; R is false, because groups within a society differ in access to wealth, education and power.

quiz.q: Which is the best indicator of inequality from a health survey?
options: Number of cricket fans living in each district
Percentage of households with access to safe sanitation
Favourite colours of residents in different towns
Total number of festivals celebrated in a year
quiz.explain: Access to basic services like sanitation varies across groups and shows inequality.
quiz.mistake: Chooses data unrelated to access to resources

teach.ask: Gappu thinks India is 'just one society'. Explain to him how India is plural and also unequal.
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Many societies inside one, and not everyone gets the same share. I see India more clearly now.
teach.nudge: You talked about diversity, but what about unequal access to things like health and education?

learn.hook: A philosopher asks how society ought to be. A sociologist asks how society actually works, and then tries to prove it with evidence.
points: Sociology is the systematic study of human social life, groups and societies, including our own behaviour as social beings.
Unlike philosophical and religious reflection, which often say how things ought to be, sociology studies how society actually works, using observation.
Peter Berger compared the sociologist to a spy: one who must report what is seen as it is, without bias or wishful thinking.

Sociology is scientific in that it follows rules of evidence that others can check. Within it there are debates: a natural-science model versus an interpretive model, and quantitative versus qualitative methods.
Sociological findings can be used in different ways by different people (governments, activists, businesses); how knowledge is used is not itself a sociological question.

example.q: Two researchers study why girls drop out of school. One counts dropout rates in 500 villages; the other lives in one village and interviews families in depth. What methods are these?
steps: Counting rates over many cases produces numbers: quantitative.
In-depth interviews and observation produce meanings and detail: qualitative.
Both follow rules of evidence that others can check.
Sociology debates which is better, and often uses both.
example.answer: The first is quantitative, the second qualitative; both are valid sociological methods.

learn.reallife: When NITI Aayog or a state government designs a scheme for school dropouts, it may use sociological findings. The research itself just describes reality; using it is a policy decision.

games.title: Match the idea
pairs: Systematic study of social life, groups and societies

games.title: Sociology or not?
items: Sociology is based on rules of evidence that others can check.
That is what makes it systematic and scientific.
Sociology mainly tells people how they ought to live.
That is closer to moral or religious reflection; sociology studies how society works.
All sociologists agree on a single method.
There are debates: natural-science vs interpretive, quantitative vs qualitative.
Sociologists study their own society and their own behaviour too.
The definition includes our own behaviour as social beings.
How sociological knowledge is used is not itself a sociological question.
Uses of knowledge depend on those who apply it.

quiz.q: Sociology is best defined as:
options: The systematic study of human social life, groups and societies
The study of how individual minds think, feel and learn
The detailed study of particular events in the distant past
The study of how an ideal society ought to be organised
quiz.explain: Sociology systematically studies social life, including our own behaviour as social beings.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sociology with psychology, history or philosophy

quiz.q: How does sociology differ from philosophical and religious reflection on society?
options: It is concerned only with religious beliefs
It ignores human values altogether in every study
It studies how society actually works, using evidence
It relies on the personal opinion of the researcher
quiz.explain: Sociology is empirical and describes reality rather than prescribing ideals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sociology's job is to give moral rules

quiz.q: Peter Berger's comparison of the sociologist to a spy stresses that the sociologist should:
options: Hide research results from the public
Report what is observed without bias
Work only for governments
Judge people's morals
quiz.explain: Like a spy reporting terrain, a sociologist must describe reality accurately.
quiz.mistake: Takes the spy image literally as secrecy

quiz.q: Sociology is called scientific mainly because:
options: It uses laboratories, test tubes and microscopes
It can predict every human action exactly and always
Its findings never change once they are published
It is bound by rules of evidence that others can check
quiz.explain: Its claims must be backed by evidence and open to checking.

quiz.q: A study that measures caste-wise literacy rates across 600 districts uses mainly:
options: Qualitative methods
Philosophical methods
Common sense
Quantitative methods
quiz.explain: Measuring rates over many units is quantitative, numerical work.

quiz.q: Which pair names a real methodological debate within sociology?
options: Sociology versus astrology as ways of predicting events
Natural-science model versus interpretive model
Village studies versus forest studies as subjects
Theory versus sports as topics for research
quiz.explain: Sociologists debate whether to study society like nature or to interpret meanings.
quiz.mistake: Picks a pair unrelated to method

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Sociologists themselves decide how their findings must be used by the government.
Reason (R): How knowledge is used is not itself a sociological question.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: A is false: findings can be used in different ways by different users. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Assumes researchers control how knowledge is used

quiz.q: Case: A researcher lives in a fishing village for a year, joining daily life and recording people's own explanations. Her approach is best called:
options: Qualitative and interpretive
Quantitative and statistical
Purely philosophical
Common-sense based
quiz.explain: Long observation and attention to meanings is a qualitative, interpretive approach.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't sociology just people's opinions about society?' Explain what sociology is and why it is systematic.
teach.praise: Tweet! Not opinions, but evidence others can check. Sociology is a careful spy, not a gossip!
teach.nudge: You said sociology studies society, but what makes it different from opinion? Think evidence.

learn.hook: 'Poor people are poor because they are lazy.' Common sense says it with confidence. Sociology asks: is that really so?
points: Common sense gives naturalistic explanations (things are 'natural' or inborn) and individualistic explanations (it is the person's own fault), e.g. blaming poverty on laziness.
Sociology explains poverty through social structure: class position, irregular or seasonal work, low wages and lack of assets.
Common sense is unreflective: it does not question where its own ideas come from. Sociology keeps asking 'is this really so?' and checks evidence.

Sociology reveals unsuspected connections. Example: after the Kargil war, compensation paid to soldiers' widows sometimes led families to press the widow to remarry within the husband's family, because under patriliny property and the widow were seen as belonging to that family.
Skill: explain an issue first in naturalistic or individual terms, then sociologically; this contrast is a common exam question.

example.q: Explain 'Girls are naturally bad at maths' first in common-sense terms and then sociologically.
steps: Common sense: it is natural, inborn (naturalistic).
Ask: is this really so? Check evidence, e.g. girls topping board exams in maths.
Sociological view: differences come from socialisation, expectations, encouragement and access to coaching.
So the cause is social, not natural.
example.answer: Common sense calls it natural; sociology shows it is produced by social expectations and opportunities.

learn.reallife: News debates often blame farmers' distress on 'bad choices'. Sociologists point to structural issues: small landholdings, debt, crop prices and monsoon dependence.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the habit of testing beliefs against evidence is why sociology questions common sense.

quiz.q: Which question is typically sociological rather than common-sense?
options: Isn't it obvious that some kids are just born to hate school?
Aren't toppers simply born smart?
Isn't poverty just fate?
Why do certain groups have higher dropout rates than others?
quiz.explain: It looks for patterns across groups and their social causes.
quiz.mistake: Picks a question that already assumes a natural or individual cause

quiz.q: Under patriliny, descent and property pass through:
options: The female line
The male line
Both lines equally
The village council
quiz.explain: Patrilineal systems trace descent and inheritance through men.

teach.ask: Gappu's uncle says 'Poor people are lazy'. Help Gappu explain why sociologists disagree with this common-sense view.
teach.praise: Tweet! Not laziness but class, wages and work patterns. Asking 'is this really so?' is my new superpower.
teach.nudge: You said the uncle is wrong, but what social causes would a sociologist point to instead?

topics.title: Intellectual ideas behind sociology: evolution and classification

learn.hook: Darwin explained how species evolve. Soon thinkers wondered: do societies 'evolve' too, like living bodies?
points: Theories of natural evolution (Charles Darwin) influenced early social thought: society was compared to a living organism whose parts (institutions) perform functions for the whole.
Accounts by early travellers and reports of colonial administrators supplied information about 'other', non-Western societies.
Societies were classified into stages: hunting-gathering, pastoral, agrarian and industrial. Western industrial society was assumed to be the most 'advanced', an assumption now criticised.
Thinkers linked with these stage and evolutionary ideas include Auguste Comte, Karl Marx and Herbert Spencer, though each built a different theory.

example.q: A textbook diagram shows society as a human body: the economy as the stomach, government as the brain. Which intellectual idea is this, and what is one criticism?
steps: Identify the comparison: society as an organism with functioning parts.
Trace the source: theories of natural evolution (Darwin) that inspired early sociology.
Criticism: such models tended to rank societies, placing the West at the top as 'most advanced'.
example.answer: It is the organic analogy drawn from evolutionary theory; it was criticised for ranking societies with the West as most advanced.

learn.reallife: Even today, people casually call some communities 'backward' and others 'advanced'. Sociology traces this habit back to 19th-century stage theories and questions it.

teach.ask: Gappu read that society is 'like a body'. Explain where this idea came from and one problem with the stage theories of society.
teach.praise: Chirp! Society as a body came from evolution theory, but ranking the West on top was a biased step.
teach.nudge: Good start. Did those old theories treat all societies equally? Think about who was called 'advanced'.

learn.hook: In 18th-century Europe a bold idea spread: use reason, not tradition, to understand everything, including human society. That idea is sociology's grandparent.
points: The Enlightenment (18th-century Europe) put reason and the individual at the centre and applied the scientific method to human affairs, not just to nature.
Poverty came to be seen as a 'social problem' that could be studied and solved, not as natural fate or divine will.
Social surveys, i.e. collecting facts about living conditions, became an early method of studying social problems.
Auguste Comte, a French thinker, is regarded as the founder of sociology. He believed sociology would contribute to human welfare.

example.q: A 19th-century reformer counts how many families in a city earn below what they need for food and rent. Which Enlightenment ideas does this reflect?
steps: The reformer uses systematic fact-gathering: a social survey.
Poverty is treated as a social problem to be measured, not as fate.
Reason and evidence are applied to human affairs, an Enlightenment idea.
example.answer: It reflects the Enlightenment belief in reason and scientific method, and the new view of poverty as a measurable social problem.

learn.reallife: India's National Sample Survey and Census continue the survey tradition: by measuring poverty, literacy and housing, the state can plan schemes rather than leave outcomes to fate.

quiz.mistake: Picks an idea the Enlightenment supported

quiz.q: Case: A state government surveys households to find which villages lack drinking water before planning pipelines. This continues which early sociological tradition?
options: Stage theory that ranks societies by progress

quiz.explain: Measuring living conditions to address problems is the social-survey tradition.

teach.ask: Gappu asks why the Enlightenment matters to sociology. Explain it, and say who is called sociology's founder.
teach.praise: Tweet! Reason applied to society, poverty as a social problem, and Comte as the founder. Got it!
teach.nudge: You missed a name! Who is regarded as the founder of sociology?

learn.hook: Imagine a weaver whose family worked the same loom at home for generations. Then a factory opens, and suddenly she must sell her labour by the hour to a stranger. Sociology was born to make sense of this shock.
points: The Industrial Revolution was centred in England (late 18th and 19th centuries) and gave rise to industrial capitalism.
Capitalism: private ownership of the means of production, profit-seeking entrepreneurs and markets; goods, services and even human labour become commodities bought and sold.
Pre-industrial life was mostly village-based, hierarchical and close-knit: peasants, artisans and landlords knew their place and each other.
Industrialisation degraded labour: workers were cut off from their guild, village and family and had to sell labour for wages.
Glossary: capitalism is a system of market enterprise based on private ownership of the means of production.

example.q: Classify each as pre-industrial or industrial-capitalist: (a) an artisan making tools for his village patron, (b) a mill hand paid hourly wages by a company.
steps: (a) Work is tied to village relations and hierarchy: pre-industrial.
(b) Labour is sold for wages in a market to a private owner: industrial capitalism.
Key difference: in (b) labour itself has become a commodity.
example.answer: (a) pre-industrial; (b) industrial capitalist, because labour is sold as a commodity.

learn.reallife: India's textile hubs like Surat and Tiruppur show capitalism at work: privately owned mills, profit-seeking firms, global markets, and workers who sell their labour for wages.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Both true; since workers lack means of production, they must sell labour for wages.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between ownership and wage dependence

quiz.q: Case: A handloom weaver who once sold cloth to village buyers now works shifts in a power-loom factory owned by a businessman. This change best illustrates:
options: A move to feudalism
The return of barter

Growth of a stateless society
quiz.explain: Private ownership, wage work and market production mark capitalism.

quiz.q: Which term means 'market enterprise based on private ownership of the means of production'?
options: Capitalism
Feudalism
Communism
Patriarchy
quiz.explain: That is the glossary definition of capitalism.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders what changed when factories came. Explain capitalism and how the life of workers changed.
teach.praise: Tweet! Private owners, profit, markets, and workers selling labour. The factory whistle makes sense now.
teach.nudge: What does a worker have to sell in capitalism, and who owns the factory?

learn.hook: A village farmer works 'until the field is done'. A factory worker works 'until the siren blows'. That switch from task time to clock time changed how humans live.
points: Industrial cities grew fast and crowded: slums, pollution, poor sanitation and new impersonal relations among strangers.

Factory production used a mechanical division of labour: each worker did a small repeated task. Marx saw it as oppressive, but also potentially liberating, because workers gathered together could organise collectively.
Clock time replaced the natural, task-based rhythms of agrarian work; the idea 'time is money' took hold.
Contrast: Britain urbanised rapidly as people moved to factory towns, while in colonial India many people were pushed back into agriculture as traditional crafts declined.
Dialectic: the interplay of opposing forces, e.g. social constraint versus individual will, or oppression versus collective resistance in the factory.

example.q: Compare a farmer in a village, a weaver in a factory and an agent in a call centre on how their work time is organised.
steps: Farmer: task-based, follows seasons and daylight.
Factory weaver: fixed shifts, siren and clock decide the day.
Call-centre agent: strict clock time, log-in hours, even timed breaks and targets per hour.
Trend: work increasingly measured by the clock, 'time is money'.
example.answer: Work moves from task-based rhythms (village) to strict clock time (factory, and even more so in a call centre).

learn.reallife: BPO and call-centre workers in Gurugram or Bengaluru often work night shifts timed to US clocks, a modern example of work organised by clock time rather than natural rhythms.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Both true; coordinated machine production required clock discipline.

quiz.explain: Production was broken into simple repeated tasks.

teach.ask: Gappu works 'whenever he feels like it'. Explain how factory work changed people's sense of time and city life.
teach.praise: Tweet! Sirens, shifts and crowded cities. The factory clock really reshaped life.
teach.nudge: And what happened to the way time was measured at work? Think about the clock.

learn.hook: Why should a student in Patna study what happened in Manchester two hundred years ago? Because the cloth, cities and colonies of that era shaped Patna too.
points: Issues like urbanisation and factory production that shaped European sociology are relevant to all modern societies, including India.
India's history is closely entangled with British capitalism and colonialism, so understanding Europe helps us understand India.
Western capitalism spread globally: enslaved Africans were taken to the Americas, and indentured Indian labourers were taken to plantations in Fiji, Surinam, the West Indies and Mauritius.
Example: the cartoonist R.K. Laxman described Mauritius's mixed population, whose make-up was shaped by colonial labour history.
Exam angle: explain why studying the origin and growth of sociology matters for understanding our own society.

example.q: A student finds that her great-great-grandfather went from Bihar to Mauritius in the 1800s. How does sociology's European story explain this?
steps: European capitalism needed labour for plantations, such as sugar in Mauritius.
After slavery ended, colonial powers recruited indentured Indian labour.
So her family history is linked to global capitalism and colonialism.
example.answer: Her ancestor's migration was part of the indentured labour system created by colonial capitalism.

learn.reallife: The Indian diaspora in Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad and Suriname celebrates Indian Arrival Day, a living reminder of how colonial capitalism moved people across oceans.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Why study Europe? I live in India!' Convince him with reasons from colonialism and capitalism.

teach.nudge: But how exactly is India's history connected to Britain? Think colonial rule and labour.

topics.title: The growth of sociology in India

learn.hook: For a British official, Indians were 'the other' across the ocean. For an Indian sociologist, as M.N. Srinivas said, 'the other' lives next door.
points: Colonialism was an integral part of modern capitalism, so Western sociology must be read in the light of the colonial experience.
Marx observed that cheap English machine-made cloth ruined India's handloom weavers.
Colonial writers wrongly saw the Indian village as unchanging, a 'survival' of early society; later research showed villages had a history and kept changing.

In the West, sociology studied modern societies and social anthropology studied 'simple' societies. In India this division blurred. As M.N. Srinivas noted, in a diverse society like India 'the other' lives next door.
Indian social anthropology moved from studying so-called 'primitive' peoples to peasants, castes, ethnic groups, classes and industrial society.

example.q: Why did the Western split between sociology and social anthropology not fit India well?
steps: In the West: sociology = modern industrial societies; anthropology = 'simple' distant societies.
India had villages and cities, castes, tribes and classes all within one nation.
An Indian researcher's 'other' (a different caste or tribe) lived close by.
So Indian scholars combined both traditions.
example.answer: Because India contained 'traditional' and 'modern' forms side by side, the two disciplines merged in Indian research.

learn.reallife: The Khadi movement of the freedom struggle answered the ruin of handloom by cheap British cloth. Today handloom clusters in places like Varanasi and Pochampally show how crafts adapted.

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: is it sociology or anthropology that Indians do? Explain how sociology grew in India and why the line blurred.
teach.praise: Tweet! In India, 'the other' is next door, so sociology and anthropology became neighbours too.
teach.nudge: You explained colonialism, but why did the two disciplines merge in India? Think of Srinivas' phrase.

topics.title: Scope of sociology; sociology and economics

learn.hook: A chat between a chaiwala and a customer, and the global trade in tea: sociology can study both, from the tiny to the planetary.
points: Scope: from micro interactions (shopkeeper and customer, teacher and student) to macro and global processes (national economy, globalisation).
Sociology is defined more by how it studies (its perspective and methods) than by what it studies; many topics are shared with other social sciences.
Boundaries between social sciences overlap; feminist theory argues strongly for interdisciplinary work.

Economics studies the production and distribution of goods and services. Sociology places economic behaviour in its social setting of norms, values, practices and interests. The political economy approach links economics with power; feminist economics counts unpaid domestic work. Pierre Bourdieu urged economists to count all the social costs of economic decisions.
Advertising and consumption show that buying is cultural: ads sell lifestyles and status, not only products.

example.q: A wedding in India costs a family ₹5 lakh. How would an economist and a sociologist study it differently?
steps: Economist: spending, savings, loans, effect on demand for gold and catering.
Sociologist: why such spending is expected, status display, caste and kinship networks, gender (dowry), norms of 'proper' weddings.
Both are needed for a full picture.
example.answer: Economics focuses on costs and markets; sociology on the norms, status and relations that make the spending socially expected.

learn.reallife: Festive-season ads for cars, phones and gold during Diwali and Akshaya Tritiya show consumption tied to culture and status, which is exactly what sociologists of consumption study.

quiz.explain: Bourdieu criticised narrow economic accounting that ignores social costs.

Assertion (A): Advertising is of interest to sociologists, not only to economists.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; because ads trade on culture and status, consumption is a sociological topic.

quiz.q: Case: A family buys a costly phone mainly so that relatives see them as 'modern'. This best shows:
options: Consumption shaped by status and culture
A purely rational decision based on price alone
A natural instinct

quiz.explain: Buying to display status is culturally shaped economic behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the social meaning of consumption

teach.ask: Gappu thinks economics already explains shopping, so why sociology? Explain the scope of sociology and how it differs from economics.
teach.praise: Tweet! Economics counts the rupees, sociology asks why we spend them the way we do. Both matter!
teach.nudge: What does sociology add that economics leaves out? Think norms, values and unpaid work.

topics.title: Sociology with political science, history and psychology

learn.hook: Why do people in one constituency vote by caste and in another by development? Political science, history, psychology and sociology would each attack this question differently.
points: Political science traditionally focused on political theory and the formal machinery of government. Political sociology studies actual political behaviour: voting patterns, parties, decision-making and gender in politics. Max Weber is a classic political sociologist.

History studies past events in concrete detail; sociology studies the contemporary or recent past and abstracts and generalises. The rise of social history (of caste, gender, everyday life) brings the two closer.
Psychology studies individual behaviour, intelligence, emotions and personality; social psychology bridges psychology and sociology.
Durkheim's study of suicide treated suicide rates as social facts: rates vary with how strongly people are integrated into social groups, not just with individual motives.
Disciplines borrow from each other: e.g. historians use sociological concepts, and sociologists use historical data.

example.q: A district's suicide rate is three times the state average. What would a psychologist and a Durkheimian sociologist each examine?
steps: Psychologist: individual factors such as stress, depression and personality.
Durkheimian sociologist: the rate as a social fact, e.g. weak social integration, debt, migration, loss of community ties.
Both views are useful; sociology looks for patterns across groups.
example.answer: The psychologist studies individual minds; the sociologist studies the social rate and its link to social integration.

learn.reallife: During Lok Sabha elections, studies such as the Lokniti-CSDS surveys analyse how caste, class, age and gender relate to voting choices: political sociology in action.

quiz.explain: Both true; by studying social patterns, social history overlaps with sociology.

quiz.q: Case: A researcher compares women's participation in panchayat elections across states before and after reservation. This research belongs most clearly to:
options: Psychology

quiz.explain: It studies gender in actual political participation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks politics is only studied through theory

quiz.q: Which is a good example of disciplines borrowing from each other?
options: A chemist measuring the pH of a water sample in a laboratory
A historian using the concept of 'class' to study a peasant revolt
A sociologist refusing to look at any historical data at all
A psychologist ignoring society while studying one person's mind
quiz.explain: Concepts and data move across disciplines.
quiz.mistake: Picks an example of no exchange

teach.ask: Gappu asks how sociology is different from history, political science and psychology. Explain with at least one example.
teach.praise: Tweet! Each discipline has its own lens, and they keep borrowing from each other. Great teamwork!
teach.nudge: You covered history, but how does sociology differ from psychology? Think of Durkheim and suicide rates.

learn.hook: An anthropologist may spend a whole year in one village, eating, farming and celebrating with families. A sociologist may survey 5,000 households in a month. Both want to understand society.
points: Anthropology has branches: physical anthropology, social or cultural anthropology, archaeology and linguistics.
Social anthropology traditionally relied on long fieldwork and ethnography (detailed description of a community's way of life), while sociology often used surveys and questionnaires with statistics.
Critique: Western anthropology had an unequal relationship with the 'natives' it studied. Colonialism also showed that 'simple' societies were never truly isolated or bounded.
Indian sociology borrows from both traditions because India mixes tradition and modernity, village and city, caste and tribe, class and community.
Activity idea: Santhal workers on Assam's tea plantations, who came from central-eastern India in colonial times, show how one group can be studied with both anthropological and sociological tools.

example.q: You want to study how Santhal tea-garden workers in Assam maintain festivals and also how their wages compare with others. Which methods would you combine?
steps: Festivals and meanings: long fieldwork, ethnography (anthropological).
Wages across estates: survey and questionnaire (sociological).
Combine both for a full picture, as Indian sociology often does.
example.answer: Combine ethnographic fieldwork with surveys, since India's mix of community and class needs both traditions.

learn.reallife: Assam's tea gardens, among the world's largest tea-producing regions, have a workforce many of whose ancestors were brought from Jharkhand, Odisha and nearby regions in colonial times; their lives are studied through both community and labour lenses.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to study tea-garden workers. Explain the difference between anthropological and sociological methods, and why Indian sociology uses both.

teach.nudge: You named one method; what does the other discipline usually use, and why does India need both?

chapters.title: Introducing Sociology: Terms, Concepts and their Use in Sociology

topics.title: Why sociology needs its own concepts

learn.hook: In everyday talk, 'group' can mean a WhatsApp chat, a crowd at a mela or your family. A sociologist cannot work with a word that slippery.
points: Everyday words like 'group', 'class' or 'society' are vague and mean different things to different people, so sociology needs precise concepts.
Concepts organise observations, allow comparison across societies and serve as the building blocks of theory.
Concepts are not neutral: they carry the stamp of the debates and social contexts in which they arose (e.g. 'class' grew out of debates on industrial capitalism).
Exam angle: 'Why do sociologists need special terms?' Answer with precision, comparison, theory building and context.

example.q: Two people say 'the middle class is growing'. One means people with a car; the other means people earning ₹5–30 lakh a year. Why is this a problem, and how does a sociologist fix it?
steps: The same word is used with two meanings: comparison becomes impossible.
A sociologist defines 'middle class' precisely (e.g. by occupation, income and education).
With a clear concept, data from different places and years can be compared.
example.answer: Vague everyday words prevent comparison; precise sociological concepts make observation and comparison reliable.

learn.reallife: When the RBI or a survey agency defines 'household' or 'urban' precisely, it can compare data across states and years. Sociology does the same with its concepts.

options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the looseness of everyday terms is why precision is needed.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect vagueness with the need for precision

options: Ancient astronomy

quiz.explain: Thinkers like Marx developed class to analyse capitalist society.
quiz.mistake: Links the concept to an unrelated context

options: Counting the number of spectators present
Asking the umpire to give a decision
Checking which team won the match
A clear definition of a social group
quiz.explain: A precise concept tells us which features a group must have.
quiz.mistake: Thinks numbers alone decide what a group is

options: Make every society look the same
Remove all the differences between cultures
Depend on personal opinion
Give a common, defined yardstick across cases
quiz.explain: A shared definition allows like-for-like comparison.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Why can't sociologists just use normal words?' Explain why special concepts are needed.
teach.praise: Tweet! Precise words, fair comparisons, solid theories. Sociology's dictionary makes sense now.
teach.nudge: You said everyday words are vague, but what do precise concepts let sociologists do? Think comparison.

topics.title: Two perspectives and the micro-macro duality

learn.hook: Look at a school. One sociologist sees teachers, students and staff cooperating to keep it running. Another sees fee-paying privilege and unequal chances. Both are looking at the same school.
points: Functionalist perspective: society is a system of interdependent parts, each performing functions that maintain order and stability.
Conflict perspective: society is marked by inequality and power; groups compete for scarce resources, and dominant groups shape institutions in their interest.
Micro level: small-scale, face-to-face interaction (a classroom, a family meal). Macro level: large-scale structures and processes (the economy, the state, globalisation).
Conceptual dualities such as individual and society, or micro and macro, are linked: individuals shape society and are shaped by it.

example.q: Apply both perspectives to the caste-based reservation of seats in colleges.
steps: Functionalist: asks how reservation helps integrate excluded groups and keeps society stable.
Conflict: asks how historic power and inequality created disadvantage and how groups contest access.
Both perspectives illuminate different aspects of the same policy.
example.answer: Functionalists stress integration and stability; conflict theorists stress inequality, power and contestation.

learn.reallife: Think of the Indian Railways: a functionalist sees millions of jobs fitting together to move the nation; a conflict theorist notices who travels in general coaches and who in AC first class.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options: Conflict

quiz.explain: Stressing integration and shared values is functionalist.

teach.ask: Gappu wants two pairs of sociology glasses. Explain the functionalist and conflict perspectives, and micro versus macro.
teach.praise: Tweet! One lens sees order, the other sees power, and I can zoom from micro to macro. Fancy glasses!
teach.nudge: You explained one perspective. What does the other focus on, order or inequality?

learn.hook: Two hundred people wait on a railway platform. Then the train is cancelled, they form a committee and march to the station master together. When did they become a group?
points: A social group: two or more people who interact regularly, share common norms and goals, and have a sense of belonging (a 'we' feeling).
An aggregate is a collection of people in the same place at the same time with no definite connection, e.g. passengers on a platform or a cinema audience.
A quasi-group lacks structure or organisation, and members may be unaware of the grouping, e.g. social classes, age groups or gender categories.
Quasi-groups and aggregates can turn into social groups when people start interacting, organising and developing common goals.
Activity skill: classify the groups you belong to (family, class, team, union) by type.

example.q: Bus passengers stuck after a breakdown start a WhatsApp group to demand compensation and meet every week. Trace the change.
steps: At first: people in one place with no lasting ties, an aggregate.
Then: they interact regularly and share a goal (compensation).
They develop a sense of 'we' and some organisation.
Now they are a social group.
example.answer: They moved from an aggregate to a social group by regular interaction, a shared goal and a sense of belonging.

learn.reallife: A crowd at Wankhede Stadium is an aggregate; the team's fan club with regular meet-ups, rules and a shared identity is a social group.

topics.title: Primary and secondary groups; community and society

learn.hook: Your family knows you hate karela. Your bank only knows your account number. That difference is the heart of primary and secondary groups.
points: Primary groups (C.H. Cooley): small, face-to-face, intimate and long-lasting; e.g. family, close friends. People relate as whole persons.
Secondary groups: larger, more impersonal, goal-oriented and formal; e.g. offices, trade unions, political parties. People relate through specific roles.
Community refers to personal, emotional, lasting ties; society or association refers to impersonal, contractual, goal-based ties.
Ferdinand Tönnies called these Gemeinschaft (community) and Gesellschaft (society or association).
Exam skill: classify the groups you belong to and compare primary and secondary groups point by point.

example.q: Classify: (a) your joint family, (b) the Residents' Welfare Association of your colony, (c) your three best friends since Class 1, (d) a political party.
steps: (a) small, intimate, lasting: primary.
(b) formal, goal-oriented, elected office-bearers: secondary.
(c) intimate, face-to-face, lasting: primary.
(d) large, formal, goal-oriented: secondary.
example.answer: (a) and (c) are primary groups; (b) and (d) are secondary groups.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways employs about 12 lakh people: a classic large, formal secondary group. Yet the gang of friends in one loco shed may be a primary group inside it.

games.title: Primary or secondary?

games.title: Match the term

quiz.q: Who introduced the concept of the primary group?
options: W.G. Sumner
C.H. Cooley
Max Weber
Robert K. Merton
quiz.explain: Cooley described primary groups as intimate face-to-face associations.
quiz.mistake: Credits Sumner, who is linked to in-groups

quiz.q: Which is a feature of a primary group?
options: Formal written rules
Very large membership
Intimate, face-to-face, lasting relationships
Relations only through specific, formal roles
quiz.explain: Primary groups involve whole-person, close ties.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a secondary group?
options: A trade union
A family
Close friends
Siblings
quiz.explain: Unions are formal, goal-oriented and impersonal.

quiz.q: Tönnies' 'Gesellschaft' refers to:
options: A close-knit village community bound together by kinship and emotion
Society or association with impersonal, contractual ties
A religious festival celebrated by a whole town
A small primary group of intimate friends
quiz.explain: Gesellschaft relations are impersonal and goal-based.

quiz.q: 'Gemeinschaft' is best translated as:
options: Market
Bureaucracy
Association
Community
quiz.explain: Gemeinschaft means community with personal, emotional ties.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): People in a secondary group usually relate to each other through specific roles.
Reason (R): Secondary groups are large and goal-oriented.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; size and goal-orientation make relations role-specific.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why size and goals matter

quiz.q: Case: Ankit chats with the bank cashier only about his deposit, but shares all his worries with his cousin. The bank and his cousin's family represent:
options: Both primary relationships
Both secondary relationships
Secondary and primary relationships respectively
Primary and secondary relationships respectively
quiz.explain: The bank relation is role-specific (secondary); the family relation is intimate (primary).
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the pair

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A political party is a secondary group.
Reason (R): Political parties are small, intimate, face-to-face groups.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: parties are large, formal and goal-oriented, which is why they are secondary groups.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a false description of parties

teach.ask: Gappu loves his nest family and also joined a bird union. Explain primary and secondary groups, and community versus society.
teach.praise: Tweet! Nest = primary and community; union = secondary and association. Tönnies would be proud of me!
teach.nudge: What makes the union different from the nest? Think size, formality and how members relate.

topics.title: In-groups, out-groups, reference and peer groups

learn.hook: India versus Pakistan in cricket: you scream for 'us'. Next week, your college plays a rival college: now your neighbour from that college is 'them'. Group boundaries shift!
points: In-group and out-group (W.G. Sumner): an in-group creates a 'we' feeling; an out-group is seen as 'they'. Boundaries can change with context.
Reference groups: groups whose standards we use to judge ourselves and whose ways we aspire to copy; we need not belong to them.
Example: during colonial rule, many middle-class Indians copied the manners, dress and speech of the British, who were their reference group.
Peer groups: a kind of primary group of people of similar age or status; peer pressure is the social influence peers exert to make one conform.

example.q: Priya's family copies the lifestyle of film stars on social media, while Priya feels pressure from classmates to buy the latest sneakers. Name the groups.
steps: Film stars: the family does not belong to them but imitates them: reference group.
Classmates: same age, close interaction, pressure to conform: peer group.
example.answer: Film stars are a reference group; classmates are a peer group exerting peer pressure.

learn.reallife: Inter-state rivalries vanish when India plays in the World Cup: the in-group widens to the whole nation, showing how boundaries shift with context.

games.title: Match the group
pairs: Standard we compare ourselves with and aspire to
People of similar age or status
Gave the in-group and out-group distinction

games.title: Which group is it?
items: We must be members of our reference group.
A reference group can be one we only aspire to join or imitate.
In-group and out-group boundaries can change with context.
Rivals in one context may be allies in another.
Peer pressure is influence from people of similar age or status.
That is how peers push one another to conform.
Colonial-era middle-class Indians copying British manners is an example of a reference group.
The British served as their standard to imitate.
A peer group is a kind of secondary group.
It is a kind of primary group.

quiz.q: The in-group and out-group distinction is associated with:
options: W.G. Sumner
C.H. Cooley
Auguste Comte
Ferdinand Tönnies
quiz.explain: Sumner distinguished 'we' groups from 'they' groups.

quiz.q: A reference group is one that:
options: We must legally join before it affects us
Always opposes us and is seen as 'they'
Is made up only of members of our family
We use as a standard and aspire to imitate
quiz.explain: We judge ourselves by its standards, whether or not we belong.

quiz.q: Colonial-era middle-class Indians copying British dress and speech illustrates:
options: An out-group being attacked
The British as a reference group
A peer group
A quasi-group
quiz.explain: They modelled their behaviour on the British.

quiz.q: A peer group is best described as:
options: A primary group of people of similar age or status
A formal organisation with written rules and officers
A group of strangers waiting together on a platform
An out-group that we see as rivals or outsiders
quiz.explain: Peers share age or status and interact closely.
quiz.mistake: Thinks peers are any people we meet

quiz.q: Case: Students from Delhi and Chennai argue about whose food is better, but cheer together for the Indian team abroad. This shows that:
options: Regional identities never matter
Out-groups are fixed forever
In-group boundaries change with context
Peer pressure is absent
quiz.explain: The 'we' expands from region to nation depending on the situation.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Peer pressure can lead a teenager to start a habit only because friends do it.
Reason (R): Peer groups exert social influence to make members conform.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the conforming influence of peers is what peer pressure is.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an example of a reference group in action?
options: A clerk copying his boss's style of dressing
A village family imitating a city family's wedding
Fans copying a cricketer's hairstyle
A child obeying traffic signals because of a fine
quiz.explain: Obeying due to a fine is formal control, not imitation of a reference group.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An out-group is always made of people from another country.
Reason (R): Out-groups are defined by a sense of 'they' in a given context.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: an out-group can be another school, team or locality. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu's friends tease him for not having a shiny feather like a famous peacock he admires. Explain in-group, out-group, reference group and peer group using this.
teach.praise: Tweet! The peacock is my reference group, my friends are my peers, and 'us vs them' keeps shifting. Wise bird now!
teach.nudge: Which group is the peacock: one you belong to or one you aspire to copy?

learn.hook: A child born in a big-city professional family and a child born to a landless labourer may be equally talented. Will they get equal chances? Stratification is the sociologist's word for why not.
points: Social stratification: structured, persistent inequality between groups ranked by their access to material or symbolic rewards.
It is a feature of society, not simply of individual differences or nature, and it is passed on across generations.
Main systems: slavery, caste, estates (feudal Europe: clergy, nobility, commoners) and class. Closed systems allow little movement; open systems allow more.
Life chances (a term associated with Max Weber): the rewards and opportunities, such as health, education and income, that come with one's position.
Social mobility is movement between positions; it is harder in closed systems like caste or estates and easier in open systems like class.

example.q: Rank these systems from most closed to most open: class, slavery, caste. Explain.
steps: Slavery: people owned by others; almost no freedom: most closed.
Caste: status ascribed by birth; very limited mobility traditionally.
Class: based on economic position; mobility possible: most open.
example.answer: Slavery, then caste, then class (most closed to most open).

learn.reallife: Data from the National Sample Survey show differences in access to higher education across social groups, a reminder that life chances differ with social position.

games.title: Closed to open

games.title: Stratification check

It persists across generations.

Life chances differ according to one's position in the stratification system.
Health, education and income vary by position.

quiz.q: Social stratification refers to:
options: Individual differences in talent and effort
Structured, persistent inequality between groups
Random differences in luck between people
An equal distribution of rewards to all
quiz.explain: It is patterned inequality built into society and lasting over time.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the most open system of stratification?
options: Caste
Slavery
Class
Estates
quiz.explain: Class allows mobility based on economic position.
quiz.mistake: Assumes caste or estates are open

quiz.q: The estate system is associated mainly with:
options: Feudal Europe
Modern Silicon Valley
Ancient tribal Africa only
Present-day Indian cities
quiz.explain: Medieval Europe had clergy, nobility and commoners as estates.
quiz.mistake: Places estates in the wrong society

quiz.q: 'Life chances' means:
options: The chances of winning a lottery or a lucky draw
The opportunities and rewards linked to social position
The biological length of a person's life only
Good or bad luck in exams and interviews
quiz.explain: Position shapes access to health, education and income.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally as luck

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Stratification persists across generations.
Reason (R): Families pass on advantages and disadvantages to their children.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Both true; inheritance of advantage is why stratification persists.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes stratification?
options: It is a social feature that ranks groups by access to rewards
It is caused only by differences in intelligence between people
It exists only in India
It applies only to individuals, not groups
quiz.explain: It is social, group-based and found in all known complex societies.
quiz.mistake: Sees stratification as natural or individual

quiz.q: Case: Two equally bright students; one from an affluent family gets private tutors and internships, the other from a poor family leaves school to work. A sociologist would explain this through:
options: Pure personal choice made by each student
Natural differences in ability between them
Differences in life chances due to stratification
Bad weather affecting one student's studies
quiz.explain: Their social positions give unequal opportunities.

quiz.q: A system where a person's position is fixed for life with almost no mobility is called:
options: Open
Flexible
Closed
Achieved
quiz.explain: Closed systems, like slavery or traditional caste, allow little movement.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks inequality is just about some birds being smarter. Explain social stratification and life chances.
teach.praise: Tweet! It's not just talent; society ranks groups and passes it down. Life chances explain so much.
teach.nudge: But is this inequality just individual, or is it built into society and inherited? Explain.

learn.hook: An IT engineer from a historically disadvantaged caste earns more than a struggling shopkeeper from a dominant caste. Which ranking matters: caste or class? Sociology says you need both, plus gender.
points: Caste (as a system of stratification): status ascribed at birth, traditionally a hereditary occupation, endogamy (marriage within the group), ranking by ideas of purity and pollution, and very limited mobility.
Class: an economic system based on wealth, income and occupation; it is open, status can be achieved, and mobility is possible.
Gender and ethnicity cut across caste and class: women within the same class or caste may face additional disadvantages.
The Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and prohibits discrimination; sociology studies how caste and class still shape opportunities.

example.q: Compare caste and class on: basis, how status is gained, mobility, and marriage rules.
steps: Basis: caste is birth and ritual status; class is economic position.
Status: caste is ascribed; class can be achieved.
Mobility: caste traditionally very limited; class allows movement.
Marriage: caste practises endogamy; class has no formal marriage rule.
example.answer: Caste is ascribed, closed and endogamous; class is economic, achievable and open.

learn.reallife: Studies of the Indian labour market show that women's participation and wages are lower than men's across classes, which is why gender is treated as a separate, cross-cutting dimension.

quiz.explain: Caste membership is determined by birth.

quiz.q: Which feature belongs to class?

quiz.explain: Class is an economic form of stratification.

options: Income and savings
Purity and pollution
Height and weight
Exam results
quiz.explain: Castes were ranked by ritual purity.
quiz.mistake: Gives an economic or physical basis

quiz.q: Why is class called an 'open' system?
options: Individuals can move up or down through achievement
Membership is decided once and for all at birth
It has no inequality between its members at all
Marriage outside one's class is strictly banned
quiz.explain: Mobility through education or occupation is possible.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Gender is a cross-cutting dimension of inequality.
Reason (R): Women within the same caste or class can face additional disadvantages compared to men.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; added disadvantages within caste and class are what make gender cross-cutting.
quiz.mistake: Treats gender as separate from caste and class

quiz.q: Which article of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability?
options: Article 21
Article 17
Article 14
Article 370
quiz.explain: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with equality (14) or life (21)

quiz.q: Case: In a city, a woman software engineer and a man in the same company with the same qualifications get different promotions. Sociologists would look at:
options: Caste as the only possible source of difference
Purely individual differences in ability
Class differences between the two employees
Gender as a dimension of inequality within class
quiz.explain: Same class position, yet gender produces a difference.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks gender within the same class

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Caste status is ascribed at birth.
Reason (R): Caste has traditionally allowed high social mobility.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: because status was fixed by birth, traditional caste allowed little mobility.
quiz.mistake: Confuses caste with the more open class system

teach.ask: Gappu asks whether caste and class are the same. Explain the differences and why gender also matters.
teach.praise: Tweet! Caste is by birth, class by economy, and gender cuts across both. Three-layer cake of inequality!
teach.nudge: You explained caste and class. Does gender add another layer of inequality?

topics.title: Status, prestige, role and role set

learn.hook: Your mother is a 'teacher' at school, a 'daughter' to your nani, a 'customer' at the sabzi mandi. Same person, many positions. Sociologists call each a status.
points: Status: a socially defined position in a group or society with attached rights and duties (mother, teacher, student).
Ascribed status is given at birth or without effort (age, sex, caste, kinship); achieved status is earned through effort (doctor, athlete, IAS officer).
Status as prestige: the social ranking or esteem attached to positions and occupations (e.g. a doctor may enjoy higher prestige than a clerk).
Role: the expected behaviour attached to a status. Status is occupied; role is played.
Role set (Robert K. Merton): the cluster of roles linked to a single status, e.g. a student relates to teachers, classmates, librarians and parents.

example.q: Identify status, role and role set: Dr. Kavita, a surgeon at AIIMS.
steps: Status: surgeon (achieved).
Role: expected behaviour, e.g. operating carefully, advising patients.
Role set: roles toward patients, nurses, junior doctors, hospital administrators and patients' families.
example.answer: Status = surgeon (achieved); role = what she is expected to do; role set = her various role relations linked to being a surgeon.

learn.reallife: Neeraj Chopra's Olympic javelin gold gave him the achieved status of Olympic champion, while his status as his parents' son is ascribed.

games.title: Ascribed or achieved?

quiz.q: Status in sociology refers to:

quiz.explain: Status is a position such as teacher or mother.

Becoming a lawyer after a law degree

quiz.explain: Kinship position is given by birth.

options: Status and role are two names for the same thing
A role is the behaviour expected of the position one holds
Roles can exist without being attached to any status
Status is a drama staged in front of an audience
quiz.explain: Role is the dynamic, behavioural side of status.
quiz.mistake: Thinks role and status are identical

quiz.q: The concept of 'role set' was given by:
options: C. Wright Mills

quiz.explain: Merton described the set of role relations linked to one status.

options: Role set
Role conflict
Ascribed status
Aggregate
quiz.explain: These are many role relations attached to one status, teacher.
quiz.mistake: Confuses role set with role conflict

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Status also has the meaning of prestige.
Reason (R): Societies rank occupations and positions differently in esteem.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; because positions are ranked in esteem, status also means prestige.
quiz.mistake: Thinks prestige is unrelated to status

quiz.q: Case: Rahul is a son, a student, a cricket captain and a nephew. How many statuses are mentioned?
quiz.explain: Son, student, captain and nephew are four statuses.
steps: Son (1), student (2), captain (3), nephew (4)

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: is 'son' a role or a status? Explain status, role, ascribed and achieved, and role set.
teach.praise: Tweet! I occupy the status 'son' and play the role of a good son. And flying champion would be achieved!
teach.nudge: You explained status; what is the role attached to it? And which statuses are ascribed or achieved?

topics.title: Role conflict, role stereotyping and changing roles

learn.hook: A doctor mother gets an emergency call on the evening of her child's school annual day. Hospital or auditorium? Welcome to role conflict.
points: Role conflict: clash of expectations arising from two or more statuses (or within one), e.g. a working mother torn between job and home duties.
Role stereotyping: fixing certain roles to certain groups, e.g. men as breadwinners and women as homemakers, or assuming nurses must be women.
Statuses and roles are not fixed by nature: they are contested and change as society changes, e.g. women as fighter pilots, men as home-makers.
Exam skill: identify your own roles and statuses and give examples of role conflict and role stereotyping.

example.q: A young man wants to become a nurse, but relatives say it is 'a woman's job'. Later, as a nurse, he must do a night shift on the day of his sister's wedding. Identify the concepts.
steps: 'Nursing is a woman's job': fixing a role to a gender, role stereotyping.
Night shift versus sister's wedding: clashing expectations from two statuses (nurse and brother), role conflict.
His career choice itself shows roles changing in society.
example.answer: Role stereotyping (nursing as women's work) and role conflict (nurse versus brother); his career shows roles can change.

learn.reallife: The Indian Air Force inducted its first women fighter pilots in 2016, a vivid example of how roles once stereotyped as 'male' can change.

games.title: Conflict or stereotype?
items: A working mother torn between office meeting and child's illness
Believing only men should be engineers
A student-athlete with an exam on match day
Assuming women should do all housework
A police officer whose brother is arrested
Expecting boys never to cry

games.title: True or false?
items: Role conflict arises when expectations of statuses clash.
That is the definition.
Roles in society never change.
Roles are contested and change over time.
Seeing men as breadwinners and women as homemakers is role stereotyping.
It fixes roles to genders.
